Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Samir presents as a 35-year-old married man, working as a tax consultant, a profession he finds increasingly difficult to manage. The man in the neat shirt and tie today is a world away from the person he was eighteen months ago, a relief worker stationed in a makeshift clinic during a brutal conflict. It was there, amidst the dust and chaos, that the foundations of his current distress were laid. He was helping a young girl with a shrapnel wound when a furious argument erupted between two men desperate for scarce medical supplies. Their shouts echoed in the small space just moments before a mortar struck the building. The world dissolved into a roar of sound, smoke, and choking dust. Samir was thrown across the room and pinned under a collapsed wall, his body instinctively curled into a tight ball. He survived, but the girl and the angry men did not.

The return to suburban American life was jarring. At first, the quiet felt like a blessing, but soon it became a canvas for the intrusive echoes of the past. The trauma lives not as a coherent story in his mind, but as a storm of disconnected fragments. He describes the memory as a confusing sequence of a child’s face, the smell of burning plastic, and the visceral feeling of his shoulders hunching as if to receive a blow. When these images surface, they are saturated with an intense, burning shame. This feeling fuels a deep-seated conviction that he should have protected the people in that clinic and that his survival was a mark of his failure. This belief that he failed has since corroded his view of the world, leaving him feeling utterly isolated and set apart from everyone he knows, including his wife.

This sense of profound difference dictates his every move. He has come to believe that joy and hope are no longer for him, so he actively avoids situations that might provoke such feelings, like anniversary dinners or friends’ celebrations. This withdrawal only serves to deepen his isolation, providing constant proof for his belief that he is alone in his experience. This retreat from the world has also been a retreat from the memory itself; by never speaking of it or allowing himself to process it, the memory has remained a raw, unchanging collection of sensory fragments—the child's face, the smell of burning plastic—as potent today as they were eighteen months ago. The conviction that he is a failure also makes him exquisitely sensitive to triggers. He scans for any sign of anger in others, so that when a client at his tax firm recently raised his voice in frustration over a filing, Samir didn't just hear a complaint; he felt a surge of pure threat. His heart hammered, his focus shattered, and the spreadsheet on his screen became a meaningless grid of numbers. He felt an overwhelming urge to cover his face with his hands and had to end the meeting abruptly. The raised voice was more than just a trigger; it was proof, delivered with brutal clarity, that his failure was so profound he couldn't even handle a simple client meeting anymore.

These encounters with triggers—the smell of a neighbour’s barbecue, a client's irritation, the mere mention of a funeral—invariably send him spiralling. The trigger ignites a feeling of immediate danger, which in turn dredges up the shameful, disordered memories of the attack. The memory confirms his failure, and the appraisal of failure amplifies his sense of threat, creating a vicious, self-sustaining loop. His life has shrunk to accommodate this cycle. He works from home as much as possible to avoid potential conflicts. Each meeting he cancels and every social event he declines becomes its own quiet reminder of the danger he perceives, effectively drawing a map of threat around the places and people he once navigated with ease. This avoidance, meant to keep him safe, has backfired, making the outside world seem even more menacing and his hypervigilance more extreme. He startles at the sound of a car door slamming and finds it nearly impossible to feel safe at night, lying awake for hours listening for disaster. Living in this constant state of high alert has made the world feel dense with potential warnings; the smell of a neighbour’s barbecue or a client's irritation are no longer just passing moments but urgent signals of danger. Feeling this unsafe, this perpetually on-edge, has quietly confirmed the conclusion he works hardest to resist: that he is permanently broken, set apart from a world where others can simply relax and feel secure. The constant state of high alert frays his concentration, making his work feel impossible and feeding the disordered, threatening nature of his trauma memories whenever they intrude.

Samir finally sought therapy after an incident last month. His wife, holding an invitation to her cousin’s wedding, had gently confronted him about his persistent refusal to engage with their life together. Seeing the hope in her eyes felt like an accusation, a reminder of a world he no longer belongs to. He retreated, leaving her standing alone in the kitchen. It was the starkness of her disappointment that broke through his wall of avoidance, forcing him to confront the chasm that had opened between his past and his present. He is here now, terrified that he is permanently broken, but holding onto a fragile hope that he can find a way to live in the world again without being a ghost.

The vignette does not state that a sense of threat causes or reinforces his negative appraisals; the memory is what confirms his belief of failure.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate that triggers directly activate his negative appraisals; this is always shown as being mediated by the trauma memory.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that a sense of threat causes or reinforces his negative appraisals; the memory is what confirms his belief of failure.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not explain how avoidance or safety behaviours lead to an increased sensitivity or hypervigilance for triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
